implementation_notes: The type system carries the router: a literal discriminant on every message makes the switch exhaustive and the never-check turns a forgotten route into a compile error, while the destinations live in a Record keyed by that discriminant so they can be injected and tested. It needs no framework, no runtime lookup table and no broker; choose it for in-process routing where the message kinds are known at build time - new kinds are added by extending the union, which is exactly the pattern's 'change only the router' rule enforced by the compiler.
pitfalls: A widened discriminant (string instead of literals) silently disables exhaustiveness.
An optional discriminant leaves arms unnarrowed, so the switch compiles but routes on the wrong shape.

variants.name: NestJS message/event patterns over a transporter
variants.implementation_notes: Nest abstracts the transporter (TCP, NATS, Redis, MQTT, Kafka) behind one interface: @MessagePattern serves request-response and @EventPattern serves fire-and-forget events, both matched on a serializable pattern value that travels with the payload, while the client side calls ClientProxy.send(pattern, payload) or emit(pattern, payload). The registered patterns are the routing table, and whether matching happens locally or in the broker depends on the transporter - so the same controller code can be routed by the platform instead of by a switch. Choose it when the process is already Nest and routing should be declarative.
pitfalls: @MessagePattern/@EventPattern only work in controllers - decorators on providers are ignored by the Nest runtime.
Handlers are matched by value, so two controllers claiming the same pattern both receive it (events fan out in parallel) instead of one replacing the other.
Transporter-specific behaviour (wildcards, ack semantics) leaks into routing tests unless the real transporter is used.
